p.src: When Second Sister You heard this, she was endlessly grateful and had no choice but to follow her. How could Madam You fail to come as well? Proper ceremony demanded that she accompany them and follow Xifeng in making the report. Xifeng said with a smile, “Just say nothing and leave the talking to me.” “Naturally,” said Madam You. “But if anything goes wrong, I shall lay the blame on you.” With that, they all went first to Grandmother Jia’s rooms.

p.src: Grandmother Jia happened to be chatting and laughing with the young ladies from the Garden to relieve her boredom. Suddenly she saw Xifeng enter with a pretty young woman and peered intently at her. “Whose child is this?” she exclaimed. “What a sweet, lovable creature!” Xifeng stepped forward and said with a smile, “Do take a careful look at her, Old Ancestress. Is she not lovely?” Then she hurriedly drew Second Sister forward. “This is your great-grandmother-in-law. Kowtow to her at once.” Second Sister promptly performed the full ceremonial obeisance, prostrating herself before rising again. Pointing to the young ladies, Xifeng continued, “This is so-and-so, and that is so-and-so. Learn who they are for now; after the ladies have seen you, you may greet them properly.” Second Sister listened, then deliberately asked each name afresh before standing to one side with lowered head. Grandmother Jia looked her up and down, then asked with a smile, “What is your surname?” “How old are you this year?” Xifeng hastily interposed with a smile, “Never mind that for now, Old Ancestress. Just tell us whether she is prettier than I am.” Grandmother Jia put her spectacles back on and ordered Yuanyang and Hupo, “Bring that child closer so I can examine her complexion.” Everyone suppressed a smile and had no choice but to urge her forward. After scrutinizing her carefully, Grandmother Jia told Hupo, “Let me see her hands.” Yuanyang then lifted her skirt. When Grandmother Jia had finished looking, she removed her spectacles and said with a smile, “She is a perfectly well-formed child. I think she is somewhat prettier than you.” At this, Xifeng smilingly dropped to her knees and related in full detail the story concocted at Madam You’s house. “Old Ancestress, you must show compassion and allow her to come in now, though she and my husband will not consummate the marriage until she has lived here for a year.” Grandmother Jia replied, “There is nothing wrong with that. “It is excellent that you should be so virtuous and generous. “Only they must wait a full year before consummating the marriage.” Xifeng kowtowed and rose, then asked Grandmother Jia to send two women with them to see the other ladies and tell them that this was the Old Ancestress’s decision. Grandmother Jia consented and had two women escort them to see Lady Xing and the others. Lady Wang had been deeply worried by the unsavory rumors about Xifeng; when she saw her act in this way, how could she fail to be pleased? Thus Second Sister You emerged into the light of day and moved into a side room. Meanwhile, Xifeng secretly had Zhang Hua instigated to demand the return of his original betrothed, promising that besides a generous dowry from this household, he would receive money to establish a home and support himself. Zhang Hua had originally possessed neither the courage nor the intention to accuse the Jia family. Later, however, he saw that Jia Rong had sent a man to coordinate testimony with him. The man’s original statement ran: “Zhang Hua first broke off the engagement. “We are all relatives. “It is true that we took her into our home, but there was never any question of marriage. “Zhang Hua owed us money and refused to pay when we pressed him; that is why he falsely accused my masters of all those things.”

p.src: The provincial censor’s office had connections with both the Jia and Wang families and had moreover accepted a bribe. It simply declared Zhang Hua a scoundrel who was trying to extort money because he was poor, refused to accept his petition, gave him a beating, and drove him out. Qing’er made arrangements for him outside, so the beating was not severe. He then urged Zhang Hua on again: “Your family arranged the engagement in the first place. If you insist only on the marriage, the authorities are certain to award her back to you.” So Zhang Hua brought another suit. Wang Xin’s people again secretly informed the censor’s office, which issued this ruling: “Zhang Hua shall repay in full, within the prescribed period, the money he owes the Jia household. As for the woman betrothed to him, he may marry and take her back when he has the means to do so.” His father was also summoned, and the ruling was formally approved in court. Qing’er had also explained matters to his father. Delighted at the prospect of acquiring both the woman and the money, the man went to the Jia household to claim her. Pretending alarm, Xifeng went to report the whole affair to Grandmother Jia. She said it was all because Cousin Zhen’s wife had handled matters carelessly and had never properly dissolved the engagement with that family, thereby provoking the suit and this official judgment. On hearing this, Grandmother Jia hastily summoned Madam You and reproached her for handling the matter improperly. “Since your sister was betrothed to someone before birth and that engagement was never properly dissolved, you have given them the chance to bring this muddled suit.” Madam You could only reply, “But they even accepted the silver. How could the dissolution not have been settled?” From the side, Xifeng added, “Zhang Hua’s deposition expressly states that he never saw any silver and never saw anyone come to arrange the matter. “His father says, ‘Her mother-in-law-to-be once mentioned it, but we never consented. “‘After her mother-in-law-to-be died, you took the girl into your household to make her a concubine.’ “With no witness to contradict them, we can only let them make whatever false claims they please. “Fortunately, Second Master Lian is away from home and has not consummated the marriage, so no real harm has yet been done. “But now that she has come here, how can we send her back without losing face?” Grandmother Jia replied, “Since the marriage has not been consummated, we cannot simply seize another man’s wife by force. That would give us a bad name. We had better send her to him. “Surely we can find another good woman somewhere.” When Second Sister You heard this, she appealed to Grandmother Jia: “My mother truly did give him ten taels of silver on such-and-such a date to dissolve the engagement, and he accepted the arrangement. “He brought this suit because poverty drove him to desperation, and now he has gone back on his word. “My elder sister did nothing wrong.” Grandmother Jia observed, “This shows how troublesome an unscrupulous commoner can be. “Since that is how matters stand, Xifeng, go and settle it.” Having no way out, Xifeng could only assent. On returning, she merely ordered someone to fetch Jia Rong. Jia Rong understood Xifeng’s intention perfectly. It would be utterly disgraceful to let Zhang Hua take Second Sister back. He therefore reported to Jia Zhen and secretly sent someone to tell Zhang Hua, “Now that you have so much silver, why insist on having the woman originally betrothed to you? “If you stubbornly persist, are you not afraid that the masters may lose their temper, find some pretext against you, and leave you without even a place to be buried? “With silver in your pocket, what good woman could you fail to find once you return home? “If you leave, you will also be given some money for your journey.”

p.src: When Zhang Hua heard this, he thought it over and decided that it was indeed a good plan. After settling the matter with his father, the two of them received about a hundred taels in all and, at the fifth watch the next morning, set out for their native place. Once Jia Rong had verified the facts, he reported to Grandmother Jia and Xifeng, saying, “Zhang Hua and his father made a false and groundless accusation, then fled for fear of punishment. The authorities know what happened and will not pursue the matter. The whole affair is settled.” On hearing this, Xifeng reflected that if Zhang Hua were made to take Second Sister You back, Jia Lian might simply spend a little more money on his return and keep her for himself, in which case Zhang Hua would hardly dare refuse. It would be safer to keep Second Sister from leaving and have her remain here as her companion; she could decide what else to do later. But no one knew where Zhang Hua was going. If he told someone else about the affair, or later used it as grounds to reopen the case, would she not have brought disaster upon herself? She should never have placed such a weapon against herself in an outsider’s hands. Her regrets knew no end, until another scheme occurred to her. She secretly ordered Wang’er to send men after Zhang Hua: either they were to accuse him of theft and prosecute him until he was put to death, or arrange his death covertly. Zhang Hua must be killed, root and branch eradicated, before her reputation could be secure. Wang’er accepted the order and left, but on returning home he thought carefully: “The man has gone, and the affair is over. Why make such a great business of it? A human life is at stake; this is no child’s play. For now I shall deceive her and consider what to do afterward.” He therefore hid outside the house for several days, then returned and told Xifeng that Zhang Hua, having several taels of silver on him, had been waylaid within the bounds of Jingkou at the fifth watch on the third day of his flight and clubbed to death by highwaymen. His father had fainted from terror at the inn, while the body was examined and buried there. Xifeng did not believe him. “If you are lying,” she said, “I shall send someone else to investigate, and when I find out, I’ll knock your teeth out!” Only then did she let the matter drop and pursue it no further. Xifeng and Second Sister You lived in extraordinary harmony, seemingly ten times more affectionate than sisters of the same blood.

p.src: One day, when Jia Lian returned after completing his business, he went first to the new house and found it quietly sealed up, with only an old caretaker left there. Jia Lian asked the reason. When the old man told him the whole story, Jia Lian could only stamp his foot in the stirrup. He had no choice but to call on Jia She and Lady Xing and report how the commission entrusted to him had been completed. Jia She was highly delighted, praised his competence, and rewarded him with a hundred taels of silver. He also gave him as a concubine a seventeen-year-old maid from his own household named Qiutong. Jia Lian kowtowed, accepted her, and was beside himself with joy. After paying his respects to Grandmother Jia and the rest of the family, he returned to see Xifeng, with an inevitably guilty look on his face. But to his surprise, Xifeng showed none of her usual expression. Instead, she came out with Second Sister You to welcome him, and they exchanged the customary greetings. When Jia Lian told them about Qiutong, a somewhat pleased and self-important expression inevitably appeared on his face. As soon as Xifeng heard, she ordered two married servants to take a carriage over and bring Qiutong back. One thorn in her heart had yet to be removed, and now another had appeared from nowhere. She could only swallow her anger and assume a pleasant face to conceal it. She ordered a banquet prepared to welcome Jia Lian home and, at the same time, took Qiutong to meet Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang, and the others. Jia Lian, too, was secretly astonished.

p.src: That day was already the twelfth of the twelfth month. Before setting out, Jia Zhen first paid homage at the ancestral shrine, then came to take leave of Grandmother Jia and the others. The members of the clan escorted him as far as the Pavilion of Parting Tears before turning back; only Jia Lian and Jia Rong accompanied him for three days and three nights before returning. Along the way, Jia Zhen exhorted them to settle down and manage the household properly. Both men assented and offered the conventional polite replies, which need not be related in detail.

p.src: Now as for Xifeng at home, there was no fault to be found with the way she treated Second Sister You outwardly; inwardly, however, she harbored other designs. Whenever they were alone, she would say to Second Sister You, “Sister, the things being said about you are most unpleasant. Even the Old Lady and the other ladies have heard that you were unchaste while still an unmarried girl and had an affair with your brother-in-law. They say, ‘He picked up a woman no one else wanted; why doesn’t he put her aside and find a better one?’” “When I heard this, I nearly fell backward with rage. I tried to discover who had said it, but could find no one.” “As the days and months go by, how are we to hold our heads up before all these servants?” “I have only landed myself with a fish head that is all bones and no meat.” After repeating this a couple of times, Xifeng once again made herself ill with anger and would take neither tea nor food. Apart from Ping’er, every maid and married servant made spiteful remarks, pointing at the mulberry while abusing the locust tree and taunting Second Sister You by insinuation. Qiutong considered herself a gift from Jia She and believed no one could presume to rival her. She looked down even on Xifeng and Ping’er, so how could she possibly tolerate Second Sister You? Whenever she opened her mouth, she would say, “A whore who fornicated first and married afterward, whom no man wanted, has come here to challenge me!” Xifeng was secretly delighted to hear this, while Second Sister You felt shame, anger, and resentment in silence. Since Xifeng was pretending to be ill, she no longer took her meals with Second Sister You. Each day she merely had food sent to Second Sister You’s room, and everything served was wretched and scarcely fit to eat. Ping’er could not bear to see this. She used her own money to procure dishes for Second Sister You, or sometimes claimed that she was taking her into the garden for amusement and had soups and other food prepared separately for her in the garden kitchen. No one dared report this to Xifeng. Once, however, Qiutong happened upon them and went to carry tales to Xifeng. “It is entirely Ping’er who has ruined your good name, madam.” “She leaves perfectly good food untouched and then sneaks into the garden to eat behind your back.” On hearing this, Xifeng cursed Ping’er: “Other people keep cats to catch mice, but my cat turns around and bites the chickens!” Ping’er dared say no more, and from then on she too had to keep her distance from Second Sister You. She secretly hated Qiutong as well, but could not give voice to it.

p.src: The young ladies in the Garden, together with Li Wan, Yingchun, Xichun, and the others, all believed that Xifeng meant well; Baoyu, Daiyu, and their circle, however, secretly worried about Second Sister You. Though none of them was in a position to interfere, whenever they saw how pitiable Second Sister You was, they would visit her and show her sympathy. Whenever she spoke with them privately, Second Sister You would shed tears and wipe her eyes, yet dared not complain. Xifeng, moreover, never revealed the slightest sign of malice. When Jia Lian came home and saw how virtuous and kind Xifeng appeared, he too ceased to pay the matter much attention. Besides, Jia She had always kept a great many concubines and maidservants, and Jia Lian had often entertained improper designs upon them, though he had never dared act. Qiutong and women like her resented the old master for being so aged and muddleheaded, greedily taking more than he could manage and needlessly keeping so many women; thus, apart from the few who knew propriety and possessed a sense of shame, some of the rest flirted and joked with the young pages at the inner gate. Some even exchanged amorous glances with Jia Lian and secretly arranged assignations, but fear of Jia She had kept him from possessing any of them. Qiutong had long had an understanding with Jia Lian, though they had never once consummated it. Now, by a fortunate turn of fate, she had actually been bestowed upon him. They were dry tinder meeting raging flame, and clung together like glue and lacquer; newly mated, they could not be parted for days on end. Jia Lian's affection for Second Sister You gradually cooled, until Qiutong alone became as dear to him as life itself. Though Xifeng hated Qiutong, she was delighted to use her first to dispose of Second Sister You while keeping herself out of it. Her plan was to “kill with a borrowed sword” and “watch the tigers fight from the mountain”: once Qiutong had destroyed Second Sister You, Xifeng would destroy Qiutong in turn. Her mind made up, whenever no one else was present she would privately admonish Qiutong: “You are young and know nothing of such matters. She is now the second wife and the darling of your master's heart. Even I yield to her in some measure. If you confront her head-on, won't you simply be courting death?” Hearing this only made Qiutong angrier. Every day she loudly hurled abuse: “Madam is mild-tempered and so virtuous, but I could never be like that. Whatever has become of Madam's former authority? Madam is magnanimous and forbearing, but I cannot tolerate a grain of sand in my eye. Just let me have one reckoning with that harlot, and then she will know her place.” Inside her room, Xifeng merely pretended that she dared not utter a word. Driven to misery, Second Sister You wept in her room and refused her food, yet dared not tell Jia Lian. The next day, Grandmother Jia saw that her eyes were red and swollen and questioned her, but she still dared not speak. Qiutong, eager to curry favor and show herself off, secretly told Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang, and the others: “She does nothing but make a spectacle of herself. Though nothing is wrong, she wails like a mourner all day long, and behind our backs she curses Second Madam and me to die early, so that she can have Second Master all to herself.” When Grandmother Jia heard this, she said, “A woman who is too delicately pretty is sure to have a jealous heart. Feng has treated her with nothing but kindness, yet she behaves so jealously and fights for favor.

u.src: The young ladies in the Garden, together with Li Wan, Yingchun, Xichun, and the others, all believed that Xifeng meant well; Baoyu, Daiyu, and their circle, however, secretly worried about Second Sister You.
Though none of them was in a position to interfere, whenever they saw how pitiable Second Sister You was, they would visit her and show her sympathy.
Whenever she spoke with them privately, Second Sister You would shed tears and wipe her eyes, yet dared not complain.
Xifeng, moreover, never revealed the slightest sign of malice.
When Jia Lian came home and saw how virtuous and kind Xifeng appeared, he too ceased to pay the matter much attention.
Besides, Jia She had always kept a great many concubines and maidservants, and Jia Lian had often entertained improper designs upon them, though he had never dared act.

Qiutong and women like her resented the old master for being so aged and muddleheaded, greedily taking more than he could manage and needlessly keeping so many women; thus, apart from the few who knew propriety and possessed a sense of shame, some of the rest flirted and joked with the young pages at the inner gate.
Some even exchanged amorous glances with Jia Lian and secretly arranged assignations, but fear of Jia She had kept him from possessing any of them.
Qiutong had long had an understanding with Jia Lian, though they had never once consummated it.

Now, by a fortunate turn of fate, she had actually been bestowed upon him. They were dry tinder meeting raging flame, and clung together like glue and lacquer; newly mated, they could not be parted for days on end.
Jia Lian's affection for Second Sister You gradually cooled, until Qiutong alone became as dear to him as life itself.

Though Xifeng hated Qiutong, she was delighted to use her first to dispose of Second Sister You while keeping herself out of it. Her plan was to “kill with a borrowed sword” and “watch the tigers fight from the mountain”: once Qiutong had destroyed Second Sister You, Xifeng would destroy Qiutong in turn.
Her mind made up, whenever no one else was present she would privately admonish Qiutong: “You are young and know nothing of such matters.
She is now the second wife and the darling of your master's heart. Even I yield to her in some measure. If you confront her head-on, won't you simply be courting death?”
Hearing this only made Qiutong angrier. Every day she loudly hurled abuse: “Madam is mild-tempered and so virtuous, but I could never be like that.
Whatever has become of Madam's former authority?
Madam is magnanimous and forbearing, but I cannot tolerate a grain of sand in my eye.
Just let me have one reckoning with that harlot, and then she will know her place.”
Inside her room, Xifeng merely pretended that she dared not utter a word.
Driven to misery, Second Sister You wept in her room and refused her food, yet dared not tell Jia Lian.
The next day, Grandmother Jia saw that her eyes were red and swollen and questioned her, but she still dared not speak.

Qiutong, eager to curry favor and show herself off, secretly told Grandmother Jia, Lady Wang, and the others: “She does nothing but make a spectacle of herself. Though nothing is wrong, she wails like a mourner all day long, and behind our backs she curses Second Madam and me to die early, so that she can have Second Master all to herself.”

p.src: Second Sister You was by nature a woman with a heart as delicate as a flower and skin as pure as snow. How could she endure such torment? After scarcely a month of suffering in silence, she fell languidly ill; her limbs grew listless, she could take neither tea nor food, and little by little she became sallow and thin. At night, whenever she closed her eyes, she saw her younger sister approach holding the paired mandarin-duck swords and say, “Sister, all your life you have been foolishly tender-hearted, and in the end it has brought you to this grief. Do not believe that jealous woman's honeyed words. Outwardly she pretends to be virtuous and kind, but inwardly she harbors treachery and cunning. In her hatred she is determined not to rest until she has brought about your death. Had I been alive, I would never have allowed you to come here; and even if you had come, I would not have let her treat you like this. Yet this too is the ordained consequence of fate. In life, you and I behaved wantonly and without virtue, bringing moral ruin and disorder upon another household; therefore this retribution has come upon us. Take my advice: use this sword to cut down that jealous woman, then come with me before the tribunal of the Disenchantment Fairy and await her judgment. Otherwise you will simply throw your life away, and no one will even pity you.” Second Sister You wept and said, “Sister, since my conduct throughout my life was already flawed, the retribution I suffer today is only just. Why should I incur yet another blood-debt by killing? Let me go on enduring it. If Heaven takes pity and lets me recover, would that not save us both?” Her younger sister laughed. “Sister, you truly are a foolish soul. Since ancient times it has been said, ‘Heaven's net is vast; though its meshes are wide, nothing slips through.’ Heaven never fails to exact repayment. Though you have repented and reformed, you have already brought a father, his sons, and brothers into the promiscuous disorder of beasts. How could Heaven allow you to live in peace?” Second Sister You wept and said, “If I am not to live in peace, that too is only right. I bear no resentment.” Hearing this, her younger sister gave a long sigh and departed. Second Sister You awoke with a start and discovered that it had been a dream. When Jia Lian came to see her, and no one else was present, she wept and told him, “I fear I shall never recover from this illness. I have been here for half a year, and I am with child, though I cannot know whether it is a boy or a girl. If Heaven takes pity and allows the child to be born, all may yet be well. Otherwise, even my own life will not be spared, much less the child's.” Jia Lian also wept and said, “Set your mind at ease. I shall find a skilled physician to treat you.” He then went out and immediately sent for a doctor.

p.src: As it happened, Imperial Physician Wang had also sought an appointment with the army, hoping to earn an hereditary title upon his return. The pages went out and instead summoned an imperial physician surnamed Hu, whose given name was Junrong. After coming in and taking her pulse, he said her menses were irregular and that she required powerful tonics. Jia Lian said, “Her courses have not come for three months, and she often retches sour fluid. I fear she may be pregnant.” Hearing this, Hu Junrong again asked the old women to have her put out her hand so that he could examine her once more. Second Sister You had no choice but to extend her hand from behind the bed-curtains once more. Hu Junrong felt her pulse for a long while, then said, “If this were pregnancy, the liver pulse should naturally be full and forceful. Yet when Wood flourishes it engenders Fire, and menstrual irregularity may likewise be caused by the Wood of the liver. A physician must be bold. I must ask madam to reveal a little of her honored face, so that I may inspect her complexion before daring to prescribe.” Jia Lian could do nothing but order the curtain opened a crack, through which Second Sister You showed her face. At the sight of her, Hu Junrong felt his soul soar to the Ninth Heaven; his whole body went numb, and he knew nothing at all. Presently the curtain was closed, and Jia Lian accompanied him outside and asked what the diagnosis was. Physician Hu replied, “It is not pregnancy, merely congealed and stagnant blood. The urgent task now is to purge the stagnant blood and clear the channels.” He then wrote out a prescription, took his leave, and departed. Jia Lian had the physician’s fee sent after him, then had the medicine prepared and administered. At midnight, however, Second Sister You was seized by unremitting abdominal pain, and to everyone’s horror she miscarried a fully formed male fetus. The bleeding would not stop, and Second Sister lost consciousness. When Jia Lian heard, he cursed Hu Junrong furiously. He sent men to summon another physician for treatment while ordering others to bring charges against Hu Junrong. On hearing of this, Hu Junrong bundled up his belongings and fled at once. The physician who came then said, “Her vital energy and blood were constitutionally deficient. Since conceiving, she must have suffered vexation that became pent up within her. That gentleman recklessly administered violent drugs. Eight or nine tenths of madam’s original vitality have now been damaged, and recovery cannot be assured soon. She must take both decoctions and pills and be kept from hearing all idle talk and troublesome affairs; only then may we hope for improvement.” Having said this, he departed. In his distress Jia Lian investigated who had summoned the man surnamed Hu; once the culprit was found, he had him beaten half to death. Xifeng appeared ten times more anxious than Jia Lian, saying only, “We are fated to be childless. After finally getting one, we had to encounter such an incompetent physician.” She burned incense and bowed before Heaven and Earth, then prayed at length: “Should illness befall me, I ask only that Sister You recover fully and conceive again to bear a son. I vow to abstain from meat for life and recite the Buddha’s name.” Jia Lian and all the others praised her when they saw this. Whenever Jia Lian was with Qiutong, Xifeng also prepared soups and drinks and had them sent to Second Sister. She also scolded Ping’er for not being blessed with children: “You are just like me.

Second Mistress’s present condition must be because we are ill-fated, or because we have offended something and brought this calamity upon her.” She then sent someone out to consult a fortune-teller and cast the trigrams. As chance would have it, the messenger returned with the fortune-teller’s words: “The offense comes from a woman born in the Year of the Rabbit.” They reckoned everyone’s birth signs and found that Qiutong alone had been born in the Year of the Rabbit, so they said she was the cause. Qiutong had lately watched Jia Lian summon physicians, administer medicines, beat servants, and curse everyone in his devotion to Second Sister You; her heart had long been steeped in a whole vat of vinegar. Now, hearing herself blamed for the offense, and with Xifeng advising, “Go and stay elsewhere for a few months, then come back,” Qiutong burst into furious tears and curses: “Why heed those blind rutters wagging their filthy tongues! She and I are like well water and river water, never encroaching on each other. How could I have harmed her? What a precious little chatterbox she is! Who knows whom she met while she was outside? Yet the moment she comes here, someone must be blamed for harming her. Without shame or proof, where did that child come from? She was merely using it to dupe that soft-eared master of ours. Even if there was a child, who knows whether its father was Zhang or Wang? Mistress may cherish that mongrel whelp, but I do not! Who cannot grow old? And who cannot bear a child? Give me a year or half a year and I will bear one—one without a trace of mixed blood in it!” Her tirade made everyone want to laugh, though none dared do so. Qiutong grew still more triumphant and deliberately went beneath Second Sister’s window, where she began loudly weeping and cursing. Hearing her, Second Sister You could not help becoming even more distressed.

p.src: That evening Jia Lian slept in Qiutong’s room. After Xifeng had gone to bed, Ping’er came to see Second Sister and quietly advised her, “Take good care of yourself and pay no heed to that beast.” Second Sister You grasped her hand and wept: “Dear sister, ever since I came here, I have owed everything to your care. On my account, you have suffered no end of undeserved vexation. If I escape with my life, I shall surely repay your kindness. But I fear I shall not survive, and then I can only wait until our next life.” Ping’er could not keep back her tears either. “When I think of it, I was the one who brought this misery upon you. I acted only out of a foolishly honest heart and never concealed anything from her. Once I heard that you were living outside, how could I possibly have kept it from her? Who could have known that all these troubles would come of it?” Second Sister You hurriedly replied, “You are wrong to say that, sister. Even if you had not told her, how could she have failed to discover it? You merely happened to tell her first. Besides, I myself was bent on coming here so that matters might be put on a proper footing. What has any of this to do with you?” The two wept together for a while. Ping’er gave her a few more words of advice, and only when the night had grown deep did she leave to rest.

p.src: Meanwhile, Second Sister You thought to herself, “My illness has already taken hold. Far from receiving the nourishment I need each day, I am being harmed instead, so I am certain I can never recover. Besides, the child is already lost, so there is nothing left to hold me here. Why endure all these petty torments? I would be better off dead and done with it. I have often heard that swallowing raw gold can make one sink into death. Would that not be cleaner than hanging or cutting my own throat?” Having resolved upon this, she struggled to her feet, opened a chest, and found a lump of raw gold whose weight she did not know. With tears in her eyes and hatred for her cruel fate, she put it into her mouth, forced her neck straight several times, and finally swallowed it. She then hurriedly dressed herself completely and put on all her ornaments before lying down on the kang. No person knew, nor did any spirit perceive it. The next morning, when the maids and married servants saw that she did not summon anyone, they were only too glad to attend to their own washing and dressing first. Xifeng and Qiutong had both gone upstairs. Pinger could not bear the sight of it and scolded the maids: “You creatures deserve to be driven only with blows and curses, since you have no hearts at all. She is ill, yet you show her no pity. She may be mild-tempered, but you ought still to show some decency. Do not go too far, joining everyone else in pushing down a collapsing wall.” At this the maids hurriedly pushed open the door and went in. They found her lying dead on the kang, fully and neatly dressed. Only then did they panic and begin shouting. Pinger came in, saw what had happened, and burst into tears. Though everyone had always feared Xifeng, they reflected that Second Sister You had truly been gentle and considerate toward her inferiors, far kinder than Xifeng. Now that she was dead, there was no one who did not grieve and shed tears; they merely dared not let Xifeng see them.

p.src: Before long, the entire household knew. Jia Lian came in, embraced the corpse, and wept without ceasing. Xifeng also made a show of weeping: “Oh, cruel-hearted sister! How could you abandon me and go, betraying all the affection I bore you?” Lady You, Jia Rong, and the others also came and wept awhile, then managed to console Jia Lian. Jia Lian then reported the matter to Lady Wang and asked permission to keep the coffin in Pear-Fragrance Court for five days before moving it to Iron Threshold Temple. Lady Wang consented. Jia Lian promptly ordered the gates of Pear-Fragrance Court opened and its main hall cleared for the bier. Thinking it undignified for the funeral procession to leave by the rear gate, Jia Lian had a large gateway newly cut through the front wall of Pear-Fragrance Court directly onto the street. Awnings were erected on both sides, and an altar was set up for Buddhist rites. A cushioned couch was spread with brocade quilts and mattresses. Second Sister You was lifted onto it and covered with a shroud. Eight pages carried her, accompanied by several married servants, along the inner wall to Pear-Fragrance Court. An astrologer had already been summoned and was waiting there. When he lifted the shroud and looked, Second Sister You’s complexion appeared lifelike, and she was even more beautiful than when alive. Jia Lian embraced her again and wailed, crying, “My darling, you died under a cloud! It was I who brought you to ruin!” Jia Rong hurried forward to console him: “Uncle, try to take it less heavily. This aunt of mine simply had no good fortune.” As he spoke, he pointed south toward the boundary wall of Prospect Garden. Jia Lian understood. Quietly stamping his foot, he said, “I was careless. Sooner or later I will get to the bottom of this, and then I will avenge you.” The astrologer reported, “The lady died precisely at the Mao hour today. The funeral cannot be held in five days; it must be either three days hence or seven. The Yin hour tomorrow will be most auspicious for placing her in the coffin.” Jia Lian said, “Three days is entirely out of the question. Make it seven. Since my uncle and elder kinsman are both away, we dare not keep so minor a funeral here too long. Once the coffin is outside, however, we shall keep it for thirty-five days and hold a grand service before sealing it away. Next year I shall take her south for burial.” The astrologer assented, wrote out the death notice, and departed. Baoyu had already come early and joined in the mourning. Members of the clan all came as well. Jia Lian hurried inside to find Xifeng and ask for silver to provide the coffin and funeral arrangements. Once Xifeng saw that the body had been carried away, she pleaded illness and said, “The Old Lady and Lady Wang say that, since I am ill and must avoid contact with the room of death, I am not permitted to go.” Thus she neither came out nor put on mourning, but went instead into Prospect Garden. Circling past the artificial hills, she reached the foot of the northern boundary wall and listened outside. After vaguely catching a word or two, she returned and reported the whole matter to Grandmother Jia in her own fashion. Grandmother Jia said, “Do not believe his nonsense. When a young person dies of consumption, what family does not simply cremate the body and scatter the ashes? Yet he means to hold a formal funeral and even break ground for a grave. Still, since she was his secondary wife, the bond of husband and wife did exist. Let her remain five or seven days, then carry her out and either cremate her or bury her in some common burial ground, and have done with it.” Xifeng smiled. “That is exactly what I think. But I do not dare advise him.”

u.src: Before long, the entire household knew.
Jia Lian came in, embraced the corpse, and wept without ceasing.
Xifeng also made a show of weeping: “Oh, cruel-hearted sister!
How could you abandon me and go, betraying all the affection I bore you?”
Lady You, Jia Rong, and the others also came and wept awhile, then managed to console Jia Lian.
Jia Lian then reported the matter to Lady Wang and asked permission to keep the coffin in Pear-Fragrance Court for five days before moving it to Iron Threshold Temple. Lady Wang consented.
Jia Lian promptly ordered the gates of Pear-Fragrance Court opened and its main hall cleared for the bier.
Thinking it undignified for the funeral procession to leave by the rear gate, Jia Lian had a large gateway newly cut through the front wall of Pear-Fragrance Court directly onto the street.
Awnings were erected on both sides, and an altar was set up for Buddhist rites.
A cushioned couch was spread with brocade quilts and mattresses. Second Sister You was lifted onto it and covered with a shroud.
Eight pages carried her, accompanied by several married servants, along the inner wall to Pear-Fragrance Court.
An astrologer had already been summoned and was waiting there. When he lifted the shroud and looked, Second Sister You’s complexion appeared lifelike, and she was even more beautiful than when alive.
Jia Lian embraced her again and wailed, crying, “My darling, you died under a cloud! It was I who brought you to ruin!”
Jia Rong hurried forward to console him: “Uncle, try to take it less heavily. This aunt of mine simply had no good fortune.”

As he spoke, he pointed south toward the boundary wall of Prospect Garden. Jia Lian understood. Quietly stamping his foot, he said, “I was careless. Sooner or later I will get to the bottom of this, and then I will avenge you.”
The astrologer reported, “The lady died precisely at the Mao hour today. The funeral cannot be held in five days; it must be either three days hence or seven.
The Yin hour tomorrow will be most auspicious for placing her in the coffin.”
Jia Lian said, “Three days is entirely out of the question. Make it seven.

ja: さんじゅうごにちかんあんち
u.src: Since my uncle and elder kinsman are both away, we dare not keep so minor a funeral here too long. Once the coffin is outside, however, we shall keep it for thirty-five days and hold a grand service before sealing it away.
Next year I shall take her south for burial.”
The astrologer assented, wrote out the death notice, and departed.
Baoyu had already come early and joined in the mourning.
Members of the clan all came as well.
Jia Lian hurried inside to find Xifeng and ask for silver to provide the coffin and funeral arrangements.

Once Xifeng saw that the body had been carried away, she pleaded illness and said, “The Old Lady and Lady Wang say that, since I am ill and must avoid contact with the room of death, I am not permitted to go.”
Thus she neither came out nor put on mourning, but went instead into Prospect Garden.

Circling past the artificial hills, she reached the foot of the northern boundary wall and listened outside. After vaguely catching a word or two, she returned and reported the whole matter to Grandmother Jia in her own fashion.

Grandmother Jia said, “Do not believe his nonsense. When a young person dies of consumption, what family does not simply cremate the body and scatter the ashes? Yet he means to hold a formal funeral and even break ground for a grave.

Still, since she was his secondary wife, the bond of husband and wife did exist. Let her remain five or seven days, then carry her out and either cremate her or bury her in some common burial ground, and have done with it.”
Xifeng smiled. “That is exactly what I think.
But I do not dare advise him.”

p.src: While they were speaking, a maid came to summon Xifeng, saying, “Second Master is waiting for you to bring him the silver.” Xifeng had no choice but to go. She asked him, “What silver? Do you not know how difficult things have become in this household lately? Our monthly allowances fall shorter every month; we have already eaten tomorrow’s grain today. Only yesterday I pawned two gold neck rings for three hundred taels, and here you are still dreaming. There are another twenty or thirty taels here. Take them if you want them.” So saying, she ordered Pinger to bring out the money and hand it to Jia Lian. Then, claiming Grandmother Jia had something to discuss with her, she left again. Jia Lian was furious but could say nothing. He had no choice but to open Second Sister You’s chests and cupboards to fetch his own private savings. When he opened them, however, not a single coin remained. There were only some broken hairpins, battered artificial flowers, and several silk garments neither new nor old, all of which Second Sister You had ordinarily worn. He could not help grieving afresh and began to weep. He wrapped them all in a bundle himself. Without calling a page or maid to carry it, he picked it up with his own hands and took it away to be burned.

p.src: Pinger was both grieved and amused. She hurriedly stole out a parcel containing two hundred taels in small silver, caught Jia Lian in a side room, and secretly handed it to him, saying, “Above all, do not let anyone hear of this. If you want to cry, there are plenty of places outside where you can do so. Why come running in here and put on a show?” Hearing this, Jia Lian said, “You are right.” He took the silver, then handed Pinger a skirt and said, “She used to wear this every day. Keep it safely for me as a remembrance.” Pinger had no choice but to conceal it and put it away herself. Jia Lian took the silver to the others, then returned and ordered men to buy coffin planks first. The fine ones were expensive, while he would accept none of middling quality. Jia Lian rode out to inspect them himself. By evening, a fine set of coffin boards was indeed carried in. It cost five hundred taels on credit, and work began that very night. Meanwhile, he assigned servants to put on mourning and keep vigil. When night fell, he did not return to the inner quarters but stayed there beside the bier.
